# Maximum likelihood estimation

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A different question: how probable are the data?

Instead of asking how far the curve is from the points, ask how probable the observed counts are, if the model with parameters $\theta$ is true. The answer is the [likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}

$$L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(y_i \mid \theta)$$

where $f(y_i \mid \theta)$ is the probability of observing $y_i$ on day $i$. The maximum likelihood estimate is the $\theta$ that makes the data most probable

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### In practice we work with the log

A product of fourteen small probabilities is a very small number. Taking logs turns it into a sum, which behaves

$$\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_{\theta} \ell(\theta) = \arg\max_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(y_i \mid \theta)$$

Most software minimises, so what we actually hand to the optimiser is the *negative* log-likelihood

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why bother? {.smaller}

- The likelihood comes from a stated probability model for the data, so every assumption is on the table
- Its shape around the maximum tells us how sure we are: standard errors and confidence intervals follow directly
- Two models fitted to the same data can be compared by their likelihoods, with AIC or BIC to keep the comparison fair
- We can say how the counts vary: Poisson, negative binomial, or anything else that matches the data

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Choosing the probability model for the data {.smaller}

The data are counts, so the natural choices are

- [Poisson:]{style="color: tomato;"} $Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$, one parameter, variance equal to the mean
- [Negative binomial:]{style="color: tomato;"} $Y_i \sim \text{NB}(\mu_i, \phi)$, with an extra parameter for how much the counts scatter beyond Poisson

For continuous measurements the usual choices are the normal, $Y_i \sim N(\mu_i, \sigma^2)$, or the log-normal, $\log Y_i \sim N(\log \mu_i, \sigma^2)$

We start with Poisson, and come back to the negative binomial at the end

## What maximum likelihood gives you {.smaller}

- Estimates that rest on a stated probability model, with standard errors and confidence intervals as part of the package
- Model comparison through AIC and BIC, as we just used it
- The freedom to describe the data honestly, whether they are Poisson counts, overdispersed counts, or something continuous
- Good large-sample properties: with enough data the estimates are as precise as any method can be

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What it asks of you {.smaller}

- A probability model for the data, which you have to choose and can get wrong
- An optimiser that needs sensible starting values and can settle in the wrong valley; we started from the least squares fit for exactly that reason
- Confidence intervals that rely on large-sample arguments, which fourteen data points may not satisfy
- No escape from identifiability: the profiles were narrow here, but only because these data are unusually clean

------------------------------------------------------------------------
